**Picasso's Blue Period**
The phase of Pablo Picasso's career (roughly 1901–1904) when he painted in somber, monochromatic blues and blue-greens. He depicted poverty-stricken, melancholy subjects such as beggars, the blind, and outcasts, and it is usually contrasted with his warmer, later "Rose Period."

**The Old Guitarist**
Picasso's most famous Blue Period painting (1903–1904), showing a gaunt, blind, bowed street musician hunched over a brown guitar, the only warm color in the picture. It hangs in the Art Institute of Chicago.

**Carles Casagemas**
Picasso's close friend, whose suicide in 1901 Picasso said prompted him to start painting in blue. Picasso painted The Death of Casagemas and Casagemas in His Coffin, and Casagemas appears as the male figure in the Blue Period painting La Vie, in which pairs of figures clutch each other in despair. The Tragedy, showing a dejected couple and child on a beach, is another work from the period.

**Ultramarine and lapis lazuli**
The most prized blue pigment of medieval and Renaissance painting, ground from the semiprecious stone lapis lazuli, mined in Afghanistan; its name means "beyond the sea." It was so expensive that it was usually reserved for the robes of the Virgin Mary. Vermeer used it for the headscarf in Girl with a Pearl Earring, and Michelangelo reportedly left The Entombment unfinished while awaiting the costly pigment.

**Prussian blue**
The first modern synthetic pigment, discovered in Berlin in the early 1700s. Imported to Japan, it transformed ukiyo-e woodblock prints, most famously Hokusai's The Great Wave off Kanagawa. A related iron compound produced the cyanotype "blueprints" long used for technical and architectural drawings.

**Yves Klein and International Klein Blue**
The French artist Yves Klein patented a deep ultramarine pigment called International Klein Blue (IKB) and used it for his series of single-color "Monochrome" paintings, such as IKB 191. He also used it in his Anthropometries, in which nude models covered in the blue paint pressed their bodies against canvas.

**Der Blaue Reiter**
"The Blue Rider," a German Expressionist group founded in Munich in 1911 by Wassily Kandinsky and Franz Marc. It was named after a Kandinsky painting of a rider, and Marc, who associated blue with spirituality and masculinity, painted The Tower of Blue Horses.

**Kind of Blue**
Miles Davis's 1959 album, the best-selling jazz album of all time and a landmark of modal jazz. It features John Coltrane and Cannonball Adderley on saxophones, Bill Evans on piano (Wynton Kelly plays on "Freddie Freeloader"), and Jimmy Cobb on drums, and it opens with "So What."

**Rhapsody in Blue**
George Gershwin's 1924 jazz-influenced piece for piano and jazz band, commissioned by bandleader Paul Whiteman for the concert "An Experiment in Modern Music." It was orchestrated by Ferde Grofé and opens with a famous rising clarinet glissando, improvised by Whiteman's clarinetist Ross Gorman. Gershwin said the piece was inspired by the rhythms of a train ride to Boston.

**Blue notes**
Notes sung or played slightly flat of standard pitch, especially the third, fifth, and seventh scale degrees. They are characteristic of the blues, the genre that originated among Black musicians in the American South, and of jazz.

**"Blue Rondo à la Turk"**
A Dave Brubeck Quartet hit from the 1959 album Time Out. Its main theme is in 9/8, grouped 2+2+2+3, a rhythm Brubeck adapted from the "aksak" asymmetrical meters he heard Turkish street musicians play.

**The Blue Boy**
Thomas Gainsborough's portrait (c. 1770) of a young man in a shimmering blue satin costume, traditionally identified as Jonathan Buttall. It is often seen as a homage to Anthony van Dyck, and it hangs at the Huntington Library in California.

**"The Blue Danube"**
Johann Strauss II's waltz "By the Beautiful Blue Danube" (1866), the most famous work by the "Waltz King." It was later used in Stanley Kubrick's 2001: A Space Odyssey.

**Blue Mosque**
The Sultan Ahmed Mosque in Istanbul, built in the early 1600s for Sultan Ahmed I. It has six minarets and is nicknamed for the blue İznik tiles that cover its interior.

**Wilton Diptych and woad**
In the late-14th-century Wilton Diptych, the right-hand panel shows the Virgin Mary and a crowd of angels dressed almost entirely in ultramarine blue. Woad was the plant-based blue dye used in medieval Europe, including for the blues of the Unicorn Tapestries.
